title: Exploring changes in the tensile properties of Fe–30Mn–8Al-1.3C (wt%) lightweight steel at 298 K and 77 K with the chemical decomposition degree
abstract: This study investigated the deformation behavior and unexpected brittle fracture of Fe–30Mn–8Al-1.3C (wt%) steel under various aging conditions (for 3 min–2 hr) and tensile temperatures (298 K and 77 K). The initial microstructures of all non-aged and aged specimens showed a single fcc matrix without κ-carbides. Despite the high stacking fault energy (SFE), tensile deformation occurred primarily through planar dislocation slip across all aging and tensile conditions due to the high friction stress caused by solute atoms, with no evidence of mechanical twinning or strain-induced phase transformation. The change in the yield strength (YS) with aging time and tensile temperature was explained by contributions of friction stress and solid-solution hardening, except for the non-aged specimen with a higher YS value owing to its extremely high vacancy concentration. To elucidate the effects of aging and tensile conditions on the ultimate tensile elongation and uniform elongation of the present steel, the variation in the Taylor lattice domain sizes was employed. At 77 K, unexpected brittle fracture was observed in specimens aged for 40 min-1 hr. This phenomenon was attributed to the interaction between the ordered structure induced by chemical decomposition and stacking faults in the solute-lean γʹ phase. As aging time increased, reductions in Al and C concentrations lowered the SFE of the γʹ phase, promoting dislocation separation into partials under high stresses at 77 K. The repulsive interactions between Al and C atoms within stacking fault regions caused widespread lattice instability, resulting in immediate fracture after yielding.
journal: Journal of Materials Research and Technology

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Face-centered cubic ( fcc ) austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C steels with high manganese (Mn; 28-33 wt%), aluminum (Al; 8-11 wt%), and carbon (C; 0.9-1.3 wt%) contents, such as Fe–31Mn–8Al-1.1C (wt%) [ 1 ], Fe–28Mn–10Al-1.0C (wt%) [ 2 ], and Fe–30Mn–9Al-0.9C (wt%) steels [ 3 , 4 ], have been considered to be novel cryogenic materials due to their representative advantages; 1) excellent mechanical properties together with the high hydrogen embrittlement resistance due to a single-phase  fcc γ -austenite, 2) superior economic efficiency compared to commercial stainless steels, and 3) low density enabled by high Al and C contents. The low density, in particular, renders these steels highly attractive for automotive and transportation areas in cryogenic industries owing to the enhancement of fuel-consumption and transportation efficiencies. However, despite these clear advantages, austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C steels face significant challenges in cryogenic applications due to a fundamental limitation of austenitic alloys,  i.e. , their inherently low mechanical properties. Therefore, to ensure the reliability of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels under cryogenic circumstances, it is necessary to suggest strategies that further enhance their intrinsic mechanical properties.

So far, numerous studies have been conducted to enhance the intrinsic mechanical properties of austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C steels through various approaches: 1) the addition of alloying elements, 2) modification of the manufacturing process, and 3) aging at specific temperatures. Regarding the first approach, the addition of alloying elements such as B [ 5 ], Cu [ 6 ], Cr [ 7 ], Mo [ 8–13 ], Nb [ 14 ], S [ 15 ], Si [ 16 ], and V [ 17 ] has been explored steadily and extensively. Among these, Mo, Nb, and V have demonstrated significant improvements in mechanical properties at room temperature without compromising ductility. For instance, Moon et al. [ 8–10 ] and Qiu et al. [ 11–13 ] independently investigated the effect of Mo additions on the tensile properties of their Fe–Mn–Al–C steels and consistently reported that 3-4 wt%Mo is the optimal concentration range for enhancing tensile strength. Huo et al. [ 14 ], Zhang et al. [ 17 ], and Xie et al. [ 18 ] observed notable improvements in tensile strength‒up to ∼200 MPa‒by adding only 0.5 wt%Nb or 0.5 wt%V. These enhancements are primarily attributed to the formation of secondary phases, particularly carbides, either within grains or along grain boundaries. These carbides contribute to matrix strengthening and grain refinement, the latter due to their pinning effect on grain boundary migration.

Second, a few new attempts have been recently made to improve the mechanical properties of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels by modifying the manufacturing process [ 19–23 ]. Mishra et al. [ 19 ], Zhang et al. [ 20 ], and Li et al. [ 21 ] processed their Fe–Mn–Al–C steel specimens through cold-rolling with a 50% thickness reduction and high-speed hammering with strains up to ∼0.75, respectively, resulting in high yield strengths exceeding ∼1300 MPa due to dislocation strengthening. Gao et al. [ 22 ] reported that increasing the hot-rolling reduction rate from 45% to 82% enhanced the tensile strength by ∼200 MPa, attributed to grain refinement  via  more active dynamic recrystallization. Zhang et al. [ 23 ] applied a warm-rolling process with reduction rates up to 65% at 623 K, achieving a high yield strength of ∼1367 MPa.

Finally, the enhancement of mechanical properties by aging is attributed to changes in chemical composition and the precipitation of particles within the matrix during additional heat treatment at moderate temperatures,  e.g. , 823 K [ 24–26 ]. Due to the preferential interaction between substitutional elements (Fe, Mn, and Al) and interstitial C atoms [ 27 ], the matrix tends to form a special precipitate known as  κ -carbide with the stoichiometry of (Fe,Mn) 3 AlC. When aging is applied at relatively low temperatures like 823 K, the matrix undergoes a progressive transformation–from a random chemical distribution,  via  spinodal decomposition, to an ordered structure characterized by the superlattice of (Fe,Mn) 3 Al Lʹ1 2  structure without C atoms. This intrinsic matrix evolution has motivated extensive research on the effects of aging on the mechanical properties of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels [ 2–4 , 16 , 24–26 , 28–33 ].

Among the three aforementioned approaches, aging offers several advantages over the others. Notably, aging can be applied as a post-treatment following alloying or manufacturing modifications. In fact, some of the studies cited above [ 5 , 8 , 16 , 17 , 19–21 , 23 ] employed aging as a final step to further enhance the mechanical properties of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels, either after adding alloying elements [ 5 , 8 , 16 , 17 ] or modifying the manufacturing process [ 19–21 , 23 ]. In addition, aging is relatively cost-effective as it does not require the use of expensive alloying elements such as Cu, Mo, Nb, and V. It also allows for precise control of mechanical properties, even in pre-manufactured components without altering their original shape. This is particularly beneficial in the context of additive manufacturing, which has recently garnered increasing attention for fabricating Fe–Mn–Al–C steels [ 34–37 ]. Given that almost all additive-manufactured products are near-net-shape, the ability to improve mechanical properties  via  aging without changing the geometry of products is a huge advantage. Thus, to ensure the reliability of austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C steels in cryogenic applications, it is crucial to first understand the effect of aging on the mechanical properties of the Fe–Mn–Al–C steel across temperatures ranging from room temperature to cryogenic temperatures, without the addition of other alloying elements.

Nevertheless, only one study has explored the effect of aging on the cryogenic tensile properties of Fe–Mn–Al–C steels. Krzanowski [ 3 ] performed tensile tests on Fe–30Mn–9Al-0.9C (wt%) specimens at room temperature, 197 K, and 77 K. The specimens were cold-rolled and subsequently annealed at 1223 K for 20 min, whereas a set of the annealed specimens was additionally aged at 823 K for 4 h. The tensile results showed that aging increased both yield strength (YS) and ultimate tensile strength (UTS), while tensile elongation (TE) still remained high (∼45%) at room temperature and 197 K for both annealed and aged specimens. However, at 77 K, the TE of the annealed specimen was preserved, whereas the aged specimen exhibited almost no TE, dropping to nearly 0%.

Given the prolonged aging time of 4 h in Krzanowski's study, it is critical to determine whether even shorter aging durations can similarly drop TE to nearly 0%. If not, there may exist a critical aging condition where maximum YS and UTS are achieved while preserving considerable TE. To explore this possibility, the present study investigates the tensile properties of Fe–Mn–Al–C steel at 298 K and 77 K under various aging conditions. 823 K was chosen as the aging temperature since it enables effective control of the chemical composition degree within a practical processing time. At a slightly higher temperature of 873 K,  κ -carbides are formed readily even after a short aging dwell time, whereas at a slightly lower temperature of 773 K, a substantially longer aging dwell time is required to obtain a noticeable variation in chemical composition [ 24 ]. Moreover, the maximum aging dwell time was set to 2 h to consider industrial applicability while suppressing  κ -carbide formation. To identify the critical aging time, small aging intervals were chosen for precise analysis.

sections.heading: Sample preparation
paragraphs: A 2 kg ingot with a chemical composition of Fe-29.75Mn-8.02Al-1.22C (wt%) was melted using a vacuum induction melting furnace. The ingot was homogenized at 1373 K for 24 h, hot-rolled at 1173 K to a thickness of ∼3.6 mm by ten rolling passes with a thickness reduction of ∼1 mm per pass, and surface-descaled to remove the oxidation layer. The hot-rolled plate with a thickness of ∼2.6 mm was then cold-rolled to reduce the thickness by 50% by thirteen rolling passes with a thickness reduction of ∼0.1 mm per pass, resulting in a sheet ∼1.3 mm thick. Tensile specimens with a gauge portion of a thickness of 1.2 mm, a width of 3 mm, and a length of 15 mm were fabricated from the cold-rolled sheet using electrical discharge machining. The schematic and detailed dimensions of the tensile specimen are provided in  Suppl. Fig. 1a . These specimens were annealed at 1273 K for 30 min in a vacuum and water-quenched to suppress chemical decomposition and  κ -carbide formation. For the aged specimens, the aging process was carried out at 823 K for various dwell times from 3 min to 2 h in a vacuum, followed by water quenching. Hereafter, non-aged and aged specimens were designated according to their dwell time,  e.g. , “0 min” for non-aged and “2 h” for 2 hr-aged specimens. Moreover, a 6 h specimen was additionally prepared based on the same aging process at 823 K for a specific purpose,  i.e. , the comparative analysis of microstructural evolution related to nano-scale  κ -carbide formation.

sections.heading: Tensile testing
paragraphs: Using non-aged and aged tensile specimens, tensile tests were carried out using a uniaxial tensile machine (Minos 100, MTDI) at 298 K and 77 K, with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 /s according to the ASTM  E8M  standard. For testing at 77 K, the schematic for the cryogenic tensile apparatus is provided in  Suppl. Fig. 1b . Specifically, the tensile specimen was mounted on the effective testing part of the tensile testing machine, followed by positioning the testing part into a dewar which allows a cooling medium, such as liquid nitrogen (LN 2 ; 77 K), to be contained. Then, LN 2  was poured into the dewar to immerse the testing part with the mounted specimen in LN 2 . The ambient temperature of the testing part was monitored using a DT-670 silicon diode sensor before and during deformation. Because the specimen was continuously immersed in LN 2  which was supplied by an external LN 2  tank, the temperature of the testing part monitored by the DT-670 sensor remained at 77 K.

The detailed microstructural evolution according to the aging dwell time at 823 K was evaluated using transmission electron microscopy (TEM; JEOL, JEM-F200) operated at 200 kV. For the specimen for the TEM, the thickness of targeted specimens was reduced down to ∼100 μm, followed by cutting as 3 mm-wide discs. Then, discs were electropolished using a Struers Tenupol twin-jet device using a 243 K-cooled mixture of methanol and 10% perchloric acid at 20 V.

For supersaturated vacancy (Va) concentration analysis, the internal friction (IF) spectra were acquired utilizing a dynamic mechanical analyzer (TA Instruments, Q800) in the three-point bending mode. Measurements were performed over a temperature range from 173 K to 573 K with a heating rate of 3 K/min, a strain amplitude of 1 × 10 −4  (0.01%), and vibrational frequency of 0.1 Hz.

sections.heading: Initial microstructure
paragraphs:
Fig. 1 
                          shows EBSD phase maps and XRD patterns of the as-annealed and as-aged specimens (0 min to 2 h). Both the EBSD and XRD results indicate that all specimens exhibit a single-phase  fcc γ -austenite structure, with a grain size of ∼13.87 μm, which remained nearly unchanged throughout the aging process. In addition, based on the Halder and Wagner method and corresponding XRD patterns, it was confirmed that the  ρ 
                         
                            ini 
                          values remained consistently low in all specimens: ∼1.15 × 10 14 /m 2  for 0 min, ∼1.50 × 10 14 /m 2  for 40 min, ∼1.35 × 10 14 /m 2  for 1 h, and ∼1.62 × 10 14 /m 2  for 2 h. Meanwhile,  κ -carbides are known to precipitate in this steel under sufficient aging conditions. Kim et al. [ 31 , 43 ] and Sato et al. [ 4 , 26 ] demonstrated that as aging conditions become more severe, XRD peaks associated with  κ -carbides appear and intensify at 2 θ  values of 23.5°, 34.0°, 41.5°, 48.5°, and 71.0°. However, as shown in  Fig. 1 e and f, the XRD patterns for all specimens show no peaks corresponding to  κ -carbides, apart from the peaks associated with the  fcc  austenite matrix. This confirms that no  κ -carbides were formed in any of the as-annealed and as-aged specimens.

To evaluate the detailed microstructural evolution related to chemical decomposition and  κ -carbide formation, TEM analysis was carried out on non-aged and aged specimens. Specifically, the non-aged specimen (0 min) and most-severely aged specimen in this study (2 h) were examined. Additionally, the specimen aged for 6 h at 823 K,  i.e. , 6 h specimen was evaluated together for the comparison.  Fig. 2 
                         a–c shows the diffraction patterns of the [001] zone axis for the 0 min, 2 h, and 6 h specimens, respectively. The corresponding dark-field (DF) TEM images based on the (100) superlattice reflection are provided in  Fig. 2 a 1 -c 1 . In all specimens, fundamental reflections of the  fcc γ -austenite matrix, such as (200), (020), and (220), were observed (highlighted by dashed white circles in  Fig. 2 a–c). Here, additional reflections besides those of the  γ -austenite matrix were observed in the aged specimens: faint {100} reflections in the 2 h specimen, and clear {100} and faint {110} reflections in the 6 h specimen (highlighted by dashed yellow circles in  Fig. 2 a–c). Line profile analysis along the sky-blue lines in  Fig. 2 a–c (see  Fig. 2 d) revealed that all specimens showed identical intensity of the (020) reflection, whereas the (010) reflection intensity increased with aging time.

The {100} superlattice reflections are attributed to L1 2 -type ((Fe,Mn) 3 Al) or Lʹ1 2 -type ( κ ʹ- or  κ -(Fe,Mn) 3 AlC 
                            x 
                          ( x  = 0–1)) atomic ordering resulting from chemical decomposition [ 44 ]. Therefore, the absence of {100} superlattice reflections in the 0 min specimen indicates a random distribution of alloying elements due to the lack of chemical decomposition. Meanwhile, the 6 h specimen showed sharp (010) reflections, indicating a high degree of atomic ordering. Moreover, considering that the presence of a C atom at the body-centered site of ordered L1 2  structure is responsible for the intensity difference between the (110) and (100) reflections [ 25 ], the large intensity gap between (100) and (110) reflections in 6 h specimen suggests a high probability of C atom occupancy at the body-centered site in the atomic-ordered region. This implies the formation of fully developed  κ -carbides (Fe,Mn) 3 AlC or the  κ ʹ-carbides (Fe,Mn) 3 AlC 
                            x 
                          with a high C concentration. These microstructural changes between the 0 min and 6 h specimens are also apparent in the DF-TEM images provided in  Fig. 2 a 1  and c 1 .

Meanwhile, the 2 h specimen ( Fig. 2 b and d) showed only faint {100} reflections, indicating a small volume fraction of second-phase particles and an incomplete transformation to  κ - or  κ ʹ-carbides. The DF-TEM image in  Fig. 2 b 1  supports the small volume fraction, showing small but well-dispersed atomic-ordering cluster regions. Considering the relatively mild aging condition (2 h at 823 K), these regions are likely long range-ordered clusters rather than  κ - or  κ ʹ-carbides, as similarly interpreted by Welsch et al. [ 44 ] based on similar reflection results. Taken together, these results suggest that for aging times shorter than 2 h at 823 K, which was adopted for this study, only short- or long-range atomic ordering occurs, while the formation of  κ -carbides or  κ ʹ-carbides does not occur.

These findings are well-matched with previous reports. According to Sato et al. [ 26 ],  κ -carbides were not formed in Fe–30Mn–9Al-0.9C (wt%) steel even after aging at 873 K for up to ∼16.1 h. Considering the higher aging temperature in their study, it is reasonable that the milder aging conditions in this study resulted only in chemical decomposition, even in the 2 h specimen. Similarly, Han et al. [ 45 ] reported no  κ -carbide formation in Fe–30Mn–8Al-1.3C (wt%) alloy aged at 823 K for 5 h based on TEM analysis, further corroborating the conclusions drawn from  Fig. 2 .

It is important to note that the specimen temperature just before water quenching differs significantly between the non-aged and aged specimens. The non-aged specimen was quenched from 1273 K, while the aged specimens were quenched from 823 K, resulting in different supersaturated Va concentrations. To experimentally confirm this, IF spectra for the 0 min-2 hr specimens were obtained in the temperature range from 173 K to 573 K ( Fig. 3 
                         ).

The spectra revealed two distinct peaks: a broad peak at 343 K (spanning 273 K-443 K) and a sharp peak at 534 K, which emerged above 473 K. Notably, the peak at 343 K was significantly smaller for the aged specimens compared with that of the non-aged (0 min) specimen, which exhibited a much higher peak. In contrast, the height of the peak at 534 K remained nearly identical across all specimens, regardless of aging conditions. Here, it should be underlined that the change in the IF spectra with aging time is not related to  ρ 
                         
                            ini 
                          due to the similarly low  ρ 
                         
                            ini 
                          values in all the as-annealed specimen (0 min) and as-aged specimens, as presented in  Fig. 1 .

Lee et al. [ 46 ] reported that C-bearing high Mn steels exhibit four peaks in their IF spectra, corresponding to different solute atom-solute atom complexes; P 1  (∼346 K) for Va-Va complexes, P 2  (∼389 K) for C-Va complexes, P 3  (∼511 K) for C–C complexes, and P 4  (∼634 K) for Mn–C complexes. In light of this report, the 0 min specimen exhibited peaks corresponding to P 1 , P 2 , and P 3 , whereas only P 3  appeared in the aged specimens. Considering that P 1  and P 2  are strongly related to Va-containing complexes, the broad peak at 343 K including P 1  and P 2  reflects Va-related contributions, while the sharp peak at 534 K is attributed to C-related complexes. The much higher intensity of the 343 K peak in the 0 min specimen compared to the aged specimens (40 min-2 hr) indicates a significantly higher Va concentration in the 0 min specimen.

sections.heading: Tensile testing results
paragraphs:
Tensile tests were conducted on 0 min-2 hr specimens at 298 K and 77 K with an initial strain rate of 1 × 10 −3 /s. The results are shown in  Fig. 4 
                         . Before describing the tensile results, it should be noted that post-uniform elongation after reaching the ultimate tensile strength (UTS) at 77 K was inconsistent without a clear systematic trend due to irregular necking behavior. Specifically, this is attributed to the fact that post-uniform elongation corresponds to the non-uniform deformation regime between the onset of necking and fracture. That is, post-uniform elongation can be strongly affected by local necking geometry, strain localization, damage evolution, and fracture initiation behavior rather than solely by the intrinsic work-hardening response of the material [ 48 ]. Therefore, elongation will be reported only up to UTS,  i.e. , uniform elongation (UE), which can be obtained by subtracting post-uniform elongation from the total elongation.

At 298 K ( Fig. 4 a and b), as aging time increased, yield strength (YS) and UTS generally increased. Since the dependence of UE at 298 K on aging time is hard to state only by the tensile curves, it will be discussed after the UE values are quantified. When the tensile temperature was lowered to 77 K ( Fig. 4 c and d), all tensile properties changed significantly across all aging conditions; YS and UTS increased, whereas UE decreased. Meanwhile, at 77 K, although YS and UTS increased with aging time, consistent with the results at 298 K, UE showed no significant variation with aging time, except for the 0 min specimen that exhibited the smallest UE. Surprisingly, in specimens aged for 40 min or longer, unexpected brittle fracture occurred immediately after yielding (inset of  Fig. 4 c).

To evaluate the variations in YS, UTS, and UE with tensile temperature and aging conditions, YS, UTS, and UE values were extracted from  Fig. 4  and plotted as a function of aging time ( Fig. 5 
                         ). At both 298 K and 77 K, YS and UTS increased with aging time. However, UE exhibited different trends: at 298 K, UE gradually decreased with aging time, while at 77 K, UE remained nearly constant until a critical aging condition (∼30 min), beyond which it dropped to nearly zero. On this account, tensile testing at 77 K was not conducted for specimens aged beyond 1 h. Thus, among the specimens fractured at 77 K, this study focuses mainly on specimens aged up to 30 min when presenting experimental results and discussion.

To determine the deformation mode, the microstructural evolution during tensile deformation at various temperatures and aging conditions was first examined using EBSD and XRD.  Fig. 6 
                          presents representative EBSD-phase maps and XRD patterns for fractured 0 min-2 hr specimens at 298 K and 77 K. The results showed that only the  fcc γ -austenite phase was detected in all specimens, even after tensile deformation to fracture. This suggests that the austenite single phase was preserved during tensile deformation up to fracture at all temperatures, without any  ε - and  α ʹ-martensite transformation.

Additionally, EBSD-image quality (IQ) and inverse pole figure (IPF) maps ( Fig. 7 
                         ) were analyzed. Although IQ maps showed numerous line patterns within grains, the IPF maps showed only minimal changes in grain orientation, except for a few orientation fragments (gray thick arrows in  Fig. 7 a–d) that exhibited orientations different from those of the parent grains. Line-profile analysis along lines 1 and 2 in  Fig. 7  revealed that the misorientation angles for line patterns were mostly below 5°, with only a few distinct peaks at 55-60°, corresponding to mechanical twins formed during tensile deformation (indicated by MT in  Figs. 7 e and f). Previous studies [ 49–51 ] showed that when mechanical twinning is the primary deformation mode, extensive twin lamellae can be readily identified in EBSD maps, even considering the inherent limitation of EBSD resolution. In contrast, the EBSD-IPF maps in this study showed relatively clean orientation contrast and only sparse twin traces ( Fig. 7 a–d). These observations suggest that the line patterns observed in all IQ maps are not attributed to deformation twins and that mechanical twinning was not the dominant deformation mode.

To evaluate the stacking fault energy (SFE) of the present steel as a function of temperature, the thermodynamic SFE model for austenitic steels proposed by Curtze et al. [ 52 ], commonly utilized for high Mn steels [ 52 , 53 ], was applied. The calculated SFE values were ∼91.25 mJ/m 2  at 298 K and ∼70.69 mJ/m 2  at 77 K, considerably higher than the threshold SFE value for mechanical twinning (∼50 mJ/m 2  [ 54 ]). These high SFE values are attributed to the high contents of Al [ 29 , 55 , 56 ] and C [ 52 , 57 , 58 ], which increase the SFE of high Mn steels. Accordingly, the high SFE values indicate that mechanical twinning is unlikely to be activated extensively in the present steel during tensile deformation at either 298 K or 77 K,  i.e. , twinning-induced plasticity was not the main deformation mode in any of the tensile tests shown in  Fig. 4 .

The slip planarity of dislocations is also a crucial factor in determining the deformation mode.  Fig. 8 
                          presents ECC images taken from 10%-strained non-aged and aged specimens. The aging conditions for this ECCI observation were selected based on the UE variation in  Fig. 5 : Whereas UE at 298 K showed a consistent dependence on aging time, that at 77 K became nearly saturated when the specimen underwent aging for above 3 min. Therefore, for 298 K, the specimens with the shortest (0 min) and longest (2 h) aging times were examined. For 77 K, specimens aged for 10 min and 30 min, representing the saturated region, were selected, along with the non-aged specimen, which exhibited the poorest tensile properties at 77 K. In addition, for each specimen, the ECC images in  Fig. 8  were acquired from a grain with a comparable crystallographic orientation, as evidenced by the similar angles (∼112°–115°) between the two operative slip traces. These images were taken in the grain interior, away from grain boundaries, to exclude the effects of neighboring grains and grain boundaries on the formation of dislocation substructures.

All specimens, regardless of aging time or tensile temperature, showed limited slip trace patterns with a few principal orientations, characteristic of Taylor lattices (TLs) [ 2 ]. At higher magnification ( Fig. 8 a), these TLs were identified as dislocation arrays aligned in a linear arrangement. This indicates that the straight-line TL patterns primarily consist of dislocation arrays, and that dislocation slip predominantly occurs through planar glide, rather than wavy glide.

In addition, at 298 K, the TL domain sizes increased significantly with aging time. In contrast, at 77 K, the 3 min and 30 min specimens exhibited similarly compact domain sizes, whereas the 0 min specimen showed larger domain sizes than both.

Finally, the dislocation behaviors during tensile deformation of the 0 min-2 hr specimens at 298 K and 0 min-30 min specimens at 77 K were additionally evaluated through EBSD-kernel average misorientation (KAM) maps. In KAM maps, yellow regions with high KAM values indicate a high density of geometrically necessary dislocations (GNDs). As shown in  Fig. 9 
                         , yellow regions in all KAM maps can be classified into two different patterns: regions along the grain boundaries, and line-shaped patterns within the grains. The former suggests that the GNDs accumulate against the grain boundaries, as these act as barriers to dislocation motion, whereas the latter indicates that GNDs concentrate along line-shaped patterns, which are not grain boundaries.

sections.heading: Changes in plastic deformation behavior in accordance with tensile temperature and aging condition
paragraphs: As shown in  Figs. 6 and 7 , plastic deformation of the present steel during tensile testing at 298 K and 77 K occurred exclusively through dislocation slip, with negligible mechanical twinning and no strain-induced phase transformation. This behavior is attributed to the high SFE values of the steel (∼91.25 mJ/m 2  at 298 K and ∼70.69 mJ/m 2  at 77 K). Additionally,  Fig. 8  shows that planar glide is the dominant dislocation motion in all specimens in the present study regardless of tensile temperature and aging conditions, rather than wavy glide. This means that the deformation mode remains unchanged regardless of changes in tensile temperature and aging conditions.

Regarding slip planarity, Hong and Laird [ 70 ] identified three key factors influencing it: SFE, short-range atomic ordering (SRO), and lattice friction induced by solute atoms. For the sake of simplicity, the long-range atomic ordering appearing in the long-aged specimens,  e.g. , the 2 h specimen, is considered to play the same role as an aggregate of SROs. An increase in SFE that suppresses the separation between leading and trailing partial dislocations facilitates cross-slip of dislocations, promoting wavy glide [ 70 ]. An increase in SRO results in glide plane softening, promoting planar slip of dislocations with dislocation arrays aligned on the same slip plane [ 31 ]. Increased lattice friction, caused by severe lattice distortion, raises the stress required for individual dislocation slip [ 60 ]. To overcome the stress, dislocations collectively glide on the same slip plane, leading to planar slip behavior.

Despite the high SFE of the present steel (∼91.25 mJ/m 2  at 298 K and ∼70.69 mJ/m 2  at 77 K), which typically favors wavy slip, ECC images showed that tensile deformation took place through planar slip. This means that the effects of SRO and lattice friction outweigh the influence of SFE on slip planarity. In particular, even the non-aged (0 min) specimen with a disordered structure,  i.e. , with a minimal degree of SRO, showed planar slip in its ECC images. That is, the lattice friction, driven by high Al, Mn, and C concentrations, is the primary factor facilitating collective dislocation glide, resulting in planar slip across all specimens. As aging time increased, the rise in the degree of SRO further enhances the propensity for planar slip.

At 298 K, this behavior aligns well with Yoo et al.’s reports [ 2 , 71 ], which showed that austenitic Fe–Mn–Al–C steels are deformed  via  planar dislocation slip without any phase transformation or mechanical twinning. Moreover, they concluded that the primary deformation mode in these steels is microband-induced plasticity (MBIP). Given that deformation at 77 K in this study exhibited similar results to 298 K, the deformation mode of the present steel with all aging conditions at both temperatures can be classified as MBIP.

The microstructural evolution during tensile deformation based on MBIP proceeds as follows [ 2 ]. At a small strain, Taylor lattices (TLs) are formed by planar dislocation glide along widely spaced slip traces with two principal orientations. As tensile strain increases, the size of the TLs continuously decreases, while the misorientation within TLs gradually increases due to the rotation of TL domains, leading to the formation of single-wall domain boundaries (DBs). Eventually, intersections between single-wall DBs and band structures consisting of a couple of single walls, referred to as microbands (MBs), are formed, subdividing grains into several subgrains. Since MBs, like grain boundaries, can act as barriers to the dislocation motion, GNDs accumulate at MBs during tensile deformation. This was reflected in the yellow line-shaped patterns within grains in all KAM maps in  Fig. 9 . That is, the progressive reduction in TL domain sizes  per se  accommodates increasing strain. Furthermore, it facilitates the TL rotation, which further accommodates strain by activating different slip systems with alternating slip senses, eventually contributing to improved UE and SHR.

Accordingly, the changes in UTS and UE with aging time, despite identical deformation modes, can be elucidated by variations in SHR, which are closely linked to TL domain sizes. To analyze this, the engineering stress-strain curves in  Fig. 4  were converted into true stress-strain curves ( Fig. 11 
                         a and b) and further processed into SHR curves ( Fig. 11 c and d). To better visualize the relationship between SHR and aging time, SHR values at true strains of 0.1 and 0.2 were extracted and plotted as a function of aging time ( Fig. 11 e and f). At 298 K ( Fig. 11 c and e), SHR decreased as aging time increased. At 77 K ( Fig. 11 d and f), all aged specimens showed nearly identical SHR, except for the 0 min specimen, which exhibited a relatively lower SHR.

This variation in SHR with aging time can be explained by the change in TL domain sizes, as shown in  Fig. 8 . At 298 K, the TL domain sizes increased with more severe aging conditions, leading to a significant difference in SHR between the 0 min and 6 h specimens. This suggests that the decrease in SHR with increasing aging time corresponds to a gradual increase in TL domain sizes. As a result, despite the steep rise in YS, the more gradual increase in UTS with aging time is attributed to a reduction in SHR caused by the increase in TL domain sizes. Additionally, the enlargement of TL domains restricts further strain accommodation, both directly and by limiting TL rotation, leading to a decrease in UE.

Meanwhile, at 77 K, the TL domain sizes were saturated at a small scale in all specimens except for the 0 min specimen, resulting in nearly identical, high SHR values. Consequently, the sharp increase in YS was directly reflected in a rise in UTS, with little variation in UE. However, the 0 min specimen, which had larger TL domain sizes than the aged specimens, exhibited significantly lower UE and UTS.

To investigate why TL domain sizes decrease as longer aging time is applied, the dislocation behavior of non-aged (0 min) and aged specimens was examined at low strain using ECCI ( Fig. 12 
                         ). For the aged specimen, the 40 min specimen was employed to capture subtle variations in dislocation behavior despite the short aging time. A strain of 1.5% was applied for this observation. In the 0 min specimen ( Fig. 12 a), well-defined dislocation arrays were observed with regular spacing between dislocations after straining. In contrast, the 40 min specimen ( Fig. 12 b) exhibited several dislocation groups consisting of a small number of dislocations, which were deemed to represent interrupted stages of dislocation-array formation. Additionally, the dislocations in these groups primarily formed pairs, as highlighted by yellow arrows.

The formation of dislocation pairs in the aged specimen is attributed to the SRO induced by the aging process [ 31 , 44 , 72 ]. Specifically, when an initial dislocation glides through the SRO structure, it locally disrupts the SRO and simultaneously leaves an antiphase boundary behind. A subsequent dislocation then follows the same path with a lower energy barrier while avoiding higher energy barriers on other slip planes, known as the glide-plane softening effect. This restores the SRO, and causes localized intensification of planar slip and the formation of periodic dislocation pairs, as seen in  Fig. 12 b. As a result, dislocation motion becomes increasingly restricted, suppressing the growth of dislocation substructures,  i.e. , TLs, and ultimately reducing the TL domain sizes with aging time at 298 K.

Meanwhile, at 77 K, the lower temperature considerably enhances the friction stress effect on slip planarity, rendering the influence of SRO negligible. Consequently, TLs form with minimal hindrance from SRO structures, resulting in consistently small TL domain sizes across all aging conditions.

In the case of the 0 min specimen deformed at 77 K, the exceptionally high Va concentration further increases the friction stress, amplifying dislocation slip planarity and restricting available slip systems. This eventually leads to the suppression of TL formation, giving rise to a decrease in TL domain sizes.

Meanwhile, when specimens aged for over 40 min were tensile-deformed at 77 K, they showed unexpected brittle fracture immediately after yielding ( Fig. 4 ), although the manufacturing process and tensile conditions except for the aging dwell time were identical to those of the other aged specimens. The abnormal tensile behavior of the 40 min-1 hr specimens can be confirmed by comparing their fracture surfaces with those of the 0 min-30 min specimens, which fractured after displaying considerable TE in their tensile curves ( Fig. 13 
                         ). Whereas the normally fractured 0 min-30 min specimens ( Fig. 13 a and b) consistently showed dimpled fracture surfaces, a mixture of intergranular (red arrows) and transgranular (yellow arrows) fracture features was observed predominantly in the abnormally fractured 40 min-1 hr specimens ( Fig. 13 c and d).

Previously, Krzanowski [ 3 ] also observed abnormal tensile fracture during tensile testing at 77 K in an Fe–Mn–Al–C steel specimen aged for 4 h at 823 K, and explained this fracture based on

However, in aged specimens with an ordered structure formed by spinodal decomposition,

                          twinning converts octahedral sites into tetrahedral sites. When twinning occurs, all C atoms in octahedral sites face at least one Al atom as a nearest neighbor, causing a permanent change in the ordering associated with special tetrahedral sites having only Fe and Mn as nearest neighbors. This results in energetically unfavorable bonds and lattice distortions associated with C atoms in tetrahedral sites, making twinning more difficult in aged specimens. Additionally, the presence of an ordered phase increases the interface energy between partial dislocations, transitioning from that of a stacking fault to a stacking fault plus an antiphase boundary. These factors inhibit permanent deformation through mechanical twinning in the ordered alloy, leading to unexpected brittle fracture in Krzanowski's 4 hr-aged specimen immediately after yielding at 77 K.

However, contrary to Krzanowski's argument, high Mn steels with high Al and C contents, like the present Fe-29.75Mn-8.02Al-1.22C (wt%) steel and Krzanowski's Fe–30Mn–9Al-0.9C (wt%) steel, are unlikely to exhibit mechanical twinning during tensile deformation at 298 K and 77 K due to their extremely high SFE. Although Krzanowski stated that tensile deformation of non-aged Fe–30Mn–9Al-0.9C (wt%) steel depends on strain-induced mechanical twinning, no direct evidence of mechanical twins was provided. The line patterns in the transmission electron microscopic image presented in Krzanowski's study more likely represent MBs, as observed in the present study, rather than mechanical twins. Furthermore, it is unlikely that special tetrahedral sites with energetically unfavorable bonds formed by mechanical twinning are the primary cause of brittle fracture at 77 K. In fact, Fe–22Mn-0.45C (wt%) steel [ 73 ], in which mechanical twinning and the formation of the aforementioned special tetrahedral sites were predominant, demonstrated considerable engineering strain of ∼60% at 77 K without brittle fracture.

Above all, it is evident that the ordered structure induced by chemical decomposition during aging is the main cause of the unexpected fracture observed in the 40 min-1 hr specimens at 77 K. This fracture is likely due to the interaction between the ordered structure ( Fig. 14 
                         a) in the solute-lean  γ ʹ phase and stacking faults. As aging progresses, the Al and C concentrations in the  γ ʹ phase decrease. Since Al and C increase the SFE of high Mn steels, their reduction lowers the SFE of the  γ ʹ phase. Additionally, the tensile temperature drop to 77 K further reduces the SFE of the steel, including  γ ʹ phase. Under specific aging conditions and at low tensile temperatures, the  γ ʹ phase reaches an SFE low enough to permit the separation of a perfect dislocation into a partial dislocation pair with a stacking fault region, even in the present steel. Here, it is noteworthy that in the  fcc  structure, the interaction energy between a C atom in an octahedral site (= a body-centered site) and an Al atom in an adjacent face-centered site is strongly repulsive [ 27 ]. In addition, the high engineering stress near yielding promotes the dislocation separation into partials. That is, through the generation of stacking faults ( Fig. 14 b), the shear displacement forcibly places Al atoms at the nearest face-centered sites of C atoms, leading to simultaneous and widespread repulsive interactions between these atoms ( Fig. 14 c). This repulsion in the stacking fault regions likely causes the brittle fracture of the 40 min-1 hr specimens soon after yielding at 77 K.

However, further study supported by quantitative parameters and robust evidence is required to establish a systematic mechanism for this unexpected fracture associated with the separation of perfect dislocations into partials with stacking faults, which is almost impossible to observe experimentally.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs:
1) 
                            When investigating the tensile properties of Fe–30Mn–8Al-1.3C (wt%) steel specimens under various aging conditions at 298 K and 77 K, except for the non-aged specimen showing poorer tensile properties, consistent dependences of YS, UTS, and UE on the aging time were observed: YS and UTS increased regardless of tensile temperature. Whereas UE at 298 K gradually decreased, that at 77 K remained constant up to an aging time of 30 min. 
                         
                         
                            2) 
                            The increase in YS with aging time at both temperatures was mainly attributed to the rise in Δ σ 
                               
                                  ss 
                                due to the change in  c  within the  γ ʹʹ phase, rather than the change in  σ 
                               
                                  fr 
                                of the  γ ʹ phase. Meanwhile, the abnormally high YS of the non-aged (0 min) specimen at 77 K was due to the extremely high Va concentration resulting from water quenching from the high quenching temperature of 1273 K. 
                         
                         
                            3) 
                            At 298 K, the growth of TLs was interrupted by the localized intensification of planar slip due to the SRO structures. This led to larger TL domain sizes with increasing aging time, giving rise to an increase in UTS and a decrease in UE. At 77 K, owing to the considerable enhancement of the friction stress effect, TLs formed with minimal hindrance from SRO structures, resulting in consistently small TL domain sizes across all aging conditions. This was ultimately responsible for an increase in UTS similar to that in YS and for the constant UE. The TL formation in the 0 min specimen was suppressed because of the high Va concentration, leading to a decrease in TL domain sizes and eventually to low UTS and UE. 
                         
                         
                            4) 
                            Specimens aged for above 40 min showed unexpected brittle fracture immediately after yielding. This fracture was thought to take place as a result of repulsive interactions between Al and C atoms due to shear displacement by the formation of stacking fault region in the solute-lean  γ ʹ phase. 
                         
                         
                            5) 
                            Considering the improvement in tensile properties of the present steel at both 298 K and 77 K up to an aging time of 30 min at 823 K, as well as the occurrence of embrittlement at 77 K after aging for more than 40 min, it can be concluded that the steel exhibits optimal tensile properties when aged for ∼30 min at 823 K.
